title: Grade 4 ENGLISH LANGUAGE — 3.3.1 Grammar in Use: Language Pattern

pages.lesson:
PAGE 1: Overview

OVERVIEW
========

Some ideas use a fixed pattern of words. In this sub-strand you will use enough followed by a noun and a to-infinitive, as in enough water to share, and you will use a lot of before a noun and a lot when no noun follows. The examples come from polite life at home and at school.

## Strand 3.0: Etiquette
Sub-strand 3.3.1: Grammar in Use: Language Pattern
Suggested lessons: 3

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) use the target language pattern in sentences correctly for fluency in speech
b) respond to questions on the language patterns in written communication
c) adopt the use of language structures for effective communication

## What this sub-strand covers
• Enough + Nominal + Infinitive
• A lot/a lot of

## Key inquiry questions
1. Why should we use correct sentences in our speech or writing?
2. How can we write sentences correctly?

## Core competencies
• Communication and Collaboration: This is promoted as the learner is able to make own sentences using appropriate language patterns correctly.
• Self-efficacy: This is enhanced as the learner gains confidence to recite poems before peers.

## Values
• Respect: This is promoted as the learner is able to appreciates other’s contributions when working to identify lines from the poem that have language patterns.
• Integrity: This is enhanced as the learner is able to demonstrate commitment to tasks both individually and when working with peers.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Peaceful coexistence: It is promoted as the learner is able to interact and socialise with peers harmoniously when working on tasks.

## Links to other learning areas
• The learner is able to relate the concept of language structures with their learning of similar concepts in Kiswahili.

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 English Language Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Theme 3.0 Etiquette, Sub-strand 3.3.1 Language Pattern

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Enough + noun + to + verb

LESSON 1: ENOUGH + NOUN + TO + VERB
===================================

## What you will learn
• Say the pattern enough + noun + to + verb.
• Build true sentences in that pattern.
• Find the pattern in a poem.

Curriculum outcomes: a) use the target language pattern in sentences correctly for fluency in speech

## Introduction
"We have water" tells you water is there. "We have enough water to offer a guest" tells you the amount is sufficient for a purpose. The pattern adds both the thing and the purpose.

## Notes
### The three parts
The pattern has three parts in a fixed order.

1. enough
2. a noun (the name of the thing you have a sufficient amount of)
3. an infinitive: to + a verb

Examples:

- enough water to offer
- enough bread to share
- enough chairs to seat
- enough time to listen
- enough words to apologise

A full sentence gives a subject and a verb before the pattern, or uses There is / There are.

- We have enough water to offer a guest.
- There is enough bread to share.
- There are enough chairs to seat the visitors.
- I have enough time to listen to you.
- She had enough courage to say sorry.

### Order matters
Say enough before the noun in this pattern. These are not the pattern:

- water enough to offer (understandable, but not the pattern you are learning)
- enough to water offer (the noun and the verb have swapped)
- enough of water to offer (do not add of before a general noun here)

The infinitive needs to. "Enough time listen" is incomplete. Say enough time to listen.

The noun can be singular or plural. Water has no plural in this sentence. Chairs is plural because we mean several chairs. Match there is with a singular or uncountable noun, and there are with a plural noun.

- There is enough time to help.
- There are enough plates to serve the guests.

### In a poem
Good Manners at Home

We have enough water to offer a guest,
We have enough bread to share at the meal.
There is a lot of kindness in this home,
And the children help a lot.

We have enough patience to listen well,
We have enough words to say sorry.
A lot of polite words make visitors glad.
Good manners matter a lot.

Four lines use enough + noun + to + verb: enough water to offer, enough bread to share, enough patience to listen, enough words to say. You will study a lot and a lot of in the next lesson. For now, find the enough lines and say them until the order feels natural.

### Speak them
Courtesy gives you true things to say. You really can have enough time to wait, enough patience to listen, and enough words to thank someone. Use the pattern for those true sentences, not only for grammar drills.

## Key words
• noun — a word that names a person, place or thing, such as water or chairs
• infinitive — the form to + verb, such as to share or to listen
• enough — as much or as many as you need

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these parts in the pattern: chairs / enough / to seat / the guests. Start with There are.

Working:
1. There are comes first because chairs is plural.
2. Enough comes before the noun.
3. The infinitive follows the noun.

Answer: There are enough chairs to seat the guests.

### Example 2
What is wrong with "She has enough to patience apologise"?

Working:
1. Enough should come just before the noun patience.
2. The infinitive is to apologise, with to before the verb.

Answer: The correct sentence is: She has enough patience to apologise.

## Activity: Find the pattern in the poem
You will need: Copies of Good Manners at Home
1. Recite the poem with a partner until you can say it smoothly.
2. Underline the lines that use enough + noun + to + verb.
3. Say what the noun is and what the infinitive is in each of those lines.
4. Construct two new sentences about etiquette using the same pattern.

## Practice
1. Complete the pattern: We have enough time ____ (listen) to our guests.
2. Choose the correct sentence: (a) There are enough plate to serve. (b) There are enough plates to serve.
3. Name the noun and the infinitive in "enough words to say".
4. Write your own sentence with enough + a noun + to + a verb.

## Summary
• The order is enough, then a noun, then to + verb.
• Use there is with one thing or a noun like water, and there are with plurals.
• The infinitive always needs to.

### Answers to practice
1. We have enough time to listen to our guests.
2. (b) There are enough plates to serve.
3. The noun is words. The infinitive is to say.
4. Any correct sentence, for example: I have enough courage to say sorry.

PAGE 3: Lesson 2: A lot and a lot of

LESSON 2: A LOT AND A LOT OF
============================

## What you will learn
• Use a lot of before a noun.
• Use a lot when no noun follows.
• Answer written questions that use both patterns from this sub-strand.

Curriculum outcomes: a) use the target language pattern in sentences correctly for fluency in speech; b) respond to questions on the language patterns in written communication

## Introduction
Learners sometimes write alot as one word, or a lots of. Neither is the form we use. The phrase is two words, a lot, and it sometimes needs of and sometimes does not.

## Notes
### A lot of + noun
A lot of means many or much. It comes before a noun.

- a lot of kindness (kindness is uncountable)
- a lot of guests (guests is a plural you can count)
- a lot of food
- a lot of polite words

There is a lot of kindness in this home.
We welcomed a lot of guests.
A lot of polite words make visitors glad.

Do not say a lots of. Lot stays singular in this phrase, even when the noun is plural: a lot of guests, not a lots of guests.

### A lot without of
When no noun follows, use a lot on its own. It often comes at the end of the sentence and tells you about the amount of an action.

- The children help a lot.
- Good manners matter a lot.
- Thank you a lot.
- She smiled a lot.

Do not add of when there is no noun. "They help a lot of" is unfinished. Either add a noun (a lot of people) or stop at a lot (they help a lot).

### Spelling
A lot is two words. Alot is not the spelling to use in your compositions.

### Questions and answers
Write full answers, not only yes or no, so the pattern appears in the answer.

- Do we have enough chairs to seat the guests? Yes, we have enough chairs to seat the guests. / No, we do not have enough chairs to seat the guests.
- Is there a lot of food? Yes, there is a lot of food.
- Do the children help a lot? Yes, they help a lot.
- Are there a lot of polite words in the poem? Yes, there are a lot of polite words in the poem.

Notice are there with a lot of plus a plural noun, and is there with a lot of plus an uncountable noun such as food or kindness.

### Both patterns in one short paragraph
We have enough cups to serve the visitors. There is a lot of water in the jug, and the children help a lot. I have enough words to say thank you.

Read that paragraph and point to each pattern before you write your own.

## Key words
• a lot of — many or much, used before a noun
• a lot — a large amount, used when no noun follows
• uncountable — a noun we do not normally count in ones, such as water or kindness

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Choose a lot or a lot of: The class smiled ____. There was ____ laughter.

Working:
1. Smiled has no noun after the phrase, so use a lot.
2. Laughter is a noun, so use a lot of.

Answer: The class smiled a lot. There was a lot of laughter.

### Example 2
Answer in a full sentence: Do you have enough time to wait?

Working:
1. Use yes or no.
2. Repeat the pattern so the answer is complete.

Answer: Yes, I have enough time to wait. (or No, I do not have enough time to wait.)

## Activity: Mark both patterns
You will need: The poem Good Manners at Home, Exercise book
1. Recite the poem again. This time underline a lot of and circle a lot where it stands alone.
2. Say which lines have a noun after a lot of, and which lines end with a lot.
3. Write answers to four questions your teacher reads, using full sentences.
4. Construct two sentences of your own: one with a lot of and one with a lot.

## Practice
1. Fill the blanks: There is ____ kindness here, and the children help ____.
2. Correct the phrase: a lots of guests.
3. Answer in a full sentence: Is there enough bread to share?
4. Why is "They smiled a lot of" incorrect?

## Summary
• Use a lot of before a noun.
• Use a lot when no noun follows.
• Write a lot as two words, and do not add an s to lot.

### Answers to practice
1. There is a lot of kindness here, and the children help a lot.
2. a lot of guests
3. Yes, there is enough bread to share. (or a true full-sentence no)
4. A lot of needs a noun. Say they smiled a lot, or they smiled a lot of smiles only if you really mean that noun.

PAGE 4: Lesson 3: Using both patterns in speech and writing

LESSON 3: USING BOTH PATTERNS IN SPEECH AND WRITING
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Combine both language patterns in a short piece of writing.
• Answer questions about the patterns in complete sentences.
• Choose these patterns on purpose when you speak.

Curriculum outcomes: b) respond to questions on the language patterns in written communication; c) adopt the use of language structures for effective communication

## Introduction
A pattern you only meet on a worksheet stays fragile. A pattern you use to thank a guest, or to describe your class, becomes part of your English. This lesson puts both patterns to work.

## Notes
### A short model
Read this paragraph aloud.

Our class has enough patience to listen when one person speaks. There are enough chairs to seat every learner. We use a lot of polite words, and those words help us a lot. I have enough courage to say sorry when I am wrong.

Patterns in the model:

- enough patience to listen
- enough chairs to seat
- a lot of polite words
- help us a lot
- enough courage to say

Nothing in the paragraph is there only as decoration. Each sentence could be said in a real classroom.

### Questions to answer in writing
Write the answer in a full sentence.

1. Do you have enough time to help a classmate today?
2. Are there enough pencils to share in your group?
3. Is there a lot of noise, or a lot of quiet, when everyone uses quiet voices?
4. Do polite words matter a lot? Why?

Sample answer for 4: Yes, polite words matter a lot because they show respect and keep the class peaceful.

Your answers should be true for your group. If there are not enough pencils, say so with the pattern: No, there are not enough pencils to share.

### Speak the patterns
With a partner, take turns.

- Ask: Do we have enough water to offer a visitor?
- Answer in the pattern.
- Ask: Do we say thank you a lot?
- Answer: Yes, we say thank you a lot. / We need to say thank you a lot more often.

Correct a slipped pattern kindly. If a partner says "enough of chairs to sit", you can reply, "Let us say enough chairs to seat our group."

### Make them a habit
Adopting a language structure means choosing it again tomorrow, not only in this exercise. When you write a story about a visitor, you might include one sentence with enough and one with a lot of. When you speak at home, "Is there enough food to share?" is both good English and good manners.

Correct sentences help people trust your meaning. A muddled pattern makes the listener rebuild your idea. Clear patterns are part of effective communication.

## Key words
• model — a correct piece of language you can follow
• adopt — to take up a habit and keep using it
• complete sentence — a sentence that gives a full answer, not a single word

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Join these ideas in one correct sentence: many polite words / they help the class greatly.

Working:
1. Many or much before a noun can be said with a lot of.
2. Greatly, at the end, can be said with a lot.

Answer: We use a lot of polite words, and they help the class a lot.

### Example 2
A learner writes "I have enough sorry to say." What should change?

Working:
1. Sorry is not the noun that fits this meaning.
2. The noun is words or courage. The infinitive is to say sorry.

Answer: I have enough words to say sorry. Or: I have enough courage to say sorry.

## Activity: Write and answer
You will need: Exercise book, The poem and the model paragraph
1. Copy the model paragraph in your best print.
2. Underline every example of enough + noun + to + verb, and of a lot or a lot of.
3. Answer the four questions in the notes in full sentences that are true for your group.
4. With a partner, ask and answer two spoken questions using the patterns. Help each other keep the word order.

## Practice
1. Rewrite correctly: We have enough of cups to serve a lots of guest.
2. Answer in a full sentence: Do polite words matter a lot?
3. Write one sentence that contains both enough + noun + to + verb and a lot of.
4. Why should you keep using these patterns after the lesson?

## Summary
• Enough + noun + to + verb shows that an amount is sufficient for a purpose.
• A lot of comes before a noun. A lot stands without one.
• Full-sentence answers keep the pattern visible and the meaning clear.

### Answers to practice
1. We have enough cups to serve a lot of guests.
2. Yes, polite words matter a lot because they show respect.
3. Any correct sentence, for example: We have enough time to welcome a lot of visitors.
4. So that your speech and writing stay clear, and so that the patterns become a habit.

REVISION QUIZ — 3.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: LANGUAGE PATTERN
========================================

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which sentence follows enough + noun + to + verb?
   A. We have water enough offer.
   B. We have enough water to offer a guest.
   C. We have to enough water offer.
   D. We enough have water a guest.

2. Which line from the poem uses the enough pattern?
   A. The children help a lot.
   B. Good manners matter a lot.
   C. We have enough bread to share at the meal.
   D. A lot of polite words make visitors glad.

3. Choose the correct sentence.
   A. There are enough plate to serve.
   B. There are enough plates to serve.
   C. There is enough plates to serve.
   D. There are a enough plates to serve.

4. Which phrase is correct?
   A. a lots of guests
   B. alot of guests
   C. a lot of guests
   D. a lot guests

5. The children help ____.
   A. a lot of
   B. a lot
   C. a lots
   D. enough of

6. There is ____ kindness in this home.
   A. a lot
   B. a lot of
   C. enough to
   D. many

7. Answer the question in a full sentence: Is there enough bread to share?

8. What is wrong with "I have enough sorry to say"?

9. Which sentence uses both patterns correctly?
   A. We have enough time to welcome a lot of visitors.
   B. We have a lot time to enough welcome.
   C. Enough we have visitors a lot of to welcome.
   D. We a lot of have enough.

10. Why do these patterns help communication?
pages.answers:
ANSWERS — 3.3.1 GRAMMAR IN USE: LANGUAGE PATTERN
========================================

1. B. We have enough water to offer a guest.
   Enough comes before the noun, and to comes before the verb.

2. C. We have enough bread to share at the meal.
   Enough bread to share is enough + noun + infinitive.

3. B. There are enough plates to serve.
   Plates is plural, so use are, and enough comes before plates.

4. C. a lot of guests
   A lot of is two words plus of, and lot has no s.

5. B. a lot
   No noun follows, so the phrase is a lot.

6. B. a lot of
   Kindness is a noun, so use a lot of.

7. Yes, there is enough bread to share.
   A full answer repeats the pattern instead of stopping at yes.

8. Sorry should be part of the infinitive or the purpose, not the noun. Say: I have enough words to say sorry.
   The noun names what you have enough of. The infinitive names the purpose.

9. A. We have enough time to welcome a lot of visitors.
   Enough time to welcome is the first pattern, and a lot of visitors is the second.

10. They show amount and purpose clearly, so the listener does not have to rebuild your meaning.
   A correct pattern is easier to understand than a muddled one.

LESSON 1: ENOUGH + NOUN + TO + VERB
===================================

## What you will learn
• Say the pattern enough + noun + to + verb.
• Build true sentences in that pattern.
• Find the pattern in a poem.

Curriculum outcomes: a) use the target language pattern in sentences correctly for fluency in speech

## Introduction
"We have water" tells you water is there. "We have enough water to offer a guest" tells you the amount is sufficient for a purpose. The pattern adds both the thing and the purpose.

## Notes

The pattern has three parts in a fixed order.

1. enough
2. a noun (the name of the thing you have a sufficient amount of)
3. an infinitive: to + a verb

- enough water to offer
- enough bread to share
- enough chairs to seat
- enough time to listen
- enough words to apologise

- We have enough water to offer a guest.
- There is enough bread to share.
- There are enough chairs to seat the visitors.
- I have enough time to listen to you.
- She had enough courage to say sorry.

- water enough to offer (understandable, but not the pattern you are learning)
- enough to water offer (the noun and the verb have swapped)
- enough of water to offer (do not add of before a general noun here)

The infinitive needs to. "Enough time listen" is incomplete. Say enough time to listen.

The noun can be singular or plural. Water has no plural in this sentence. Chairs is plural because we mean several chairs. Match there is with a singular or uncountable noun, and there are with a plural noun.

- There is enough time to help.
- There are enough plates to serve the guests.

### In a poem
Good Manners at Home

We have enough water to offer a guest,
We have enough bread to share at the meal.
There is a lot of kindness in this home,
And the children help a lot.

We have enough patience to listen well,

A lot of polite words make visitors glad.

• noun — a word that names a person, place or thing, such as water or chairs
• infinitive — the form to + verb, such as to share or to listen

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Put these parts in the pattern: chairs / enough / to seat / the guests. Start with There are.

Working:
1. There are comes first because chairs is plural.
2. Enough comes before the noun.
3. The infinitive follows the noun.

Answer: There are enough chairs to seat the guests.

1. Enough should come just before the noun patience.

Answer: The correct sentence is: She has enough patience to apologise.

You will need: Copies of Good Manners at Home
1. Recite the poem with a partner until you can say it smoothly.
2. Underline the lines that use enough + noun + to + verb.
3. Say what the noun is and what the infinitive is in each of those lines.
4. Construct two new sentences about etiquette using the same pattern.

1. Complete the pattern: We have enough time ____ (listen) to our guests.
2. Choose the correct sentence: (a) There are enough plate to serve. (b) There are enough plates to serve.
3. Name the noun and the infinitive in "enough words to say".
4. Write your own sentence with enough + a noun + to + a verb.

• Use there is with one thing or a noun like water, and there are with plurals.

2. (b) There are enough plates to serve.
3. The noun is words. The infinitive is to say.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: A lot and a lot of
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: A LOT AND A LOT OF
============================

## What you will learn
• Use a lot of before a noun.
• Use a lot when no noun follows.
• Answer written questions that use both patterns from this sub-strand.

Curriculum outcomes: a) use the target language pattern in sentences correctly for fluency in speech; b) respond to questions on the language patterns in written communication

## Introduction
Learners sometimes write alot as one word, or a lots of. Neither is the form we use. The phrase is two words, a lot, and it sometimes needs of and sometimes does not.

## Notes
### A lot of + noun
A lot of means many or much. It comes before a noun.

- a lot of kindness (kindness is uncountable)
- a lot of guests (guests is a plural you can count)
- a lot of food
- a lot of polite words

There is a lot of kindness in this home.
We welcomed a lot of guests.
A lot of polite words make visitors glad.

Do not say a lots of. Lot stays singular in this phrase, even when the noun is plural: a lot of guests, not a lots of guests.

### A lot without of
When no noun follows, use a lot on its own. It often comes at the end of the sentence and tells you about the amount of an action.

- The children help a lot.
- Good manners matter a lot.
- Thank you a lot.
- She smiled a lot.

Do not add of when there is no noun. "They help a lot of" is unfinished. Either add a noun (a lot of people) or stop at a lot (they help a lot).

### Spelling
A lot is two words. Alot is not the spelling to use in your compositions.

### Questions and answers
Write full answers, not only yes or no, so the pattern appears in the answer.

- Do we have enough chairs to seat the guests? Yes, we have enough chairs to seat the guests. / No, we do not have enough chairs to seat the guests.
- Is there a lot of food? Yes, there is a lot of food.
- Do the children help a lot? Yes, they help a lot.
- Are there a lot of polite words in the poem? Yes, there are a lot of polite words in the poem.

Notice are there with a lot of plus a plural noun, and is there with a lot of plus an uncountable noun such as food or kindness.

### Both patterns in one short paragraph
We have enough cups to serve the visitors. There is a lot of water in the jug, and the children help a lot. I have enough words to say thank you.

Read that paragraph and point to each pattern before you write your own.

## Key words
• a lot of — many or much, used before a noun
• a lot — a large amount, used when no noun follows
• uncountable — a noun we do not normally count in ones, such as water or kindness

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Choose a lot or a lot of: The class smiled ____. There was ____ laughter.

Working:
1. Smiled has no noun after the phrase, so use a lot.
2. Laughter is a noun, so use a lot of.

Answer: The class smiled a lot. There was a lot of laughter.

### Example 2
Answer in a full sentence: Do you have enough time to wait?

Working:
1. Use yes or no.
2. Repeat the pattern so the answer is complete.

Answer: Yes, I have enough time to wait. (or No, I do not have enough time to wait.)

## Activity: Mark both patterns
You will need: The poem Good Manners at Home, Exercise book
1. Recite the poem again. This time underline a lot of and circle a lot where it stands alone.
2. Say which lines have a noun after a lot of, and which lines end with a lot.
3. Write answers to four questions your teacher reads, using full sentences.
4. Construct two sentences of your own: one with a lot of and one with a lot.

## Practice
1. Fill the blanks: There is ____ kindness here, and the children help ____.
2. Correct the phrase: a lots of guests.
3. Answer in a full sentence: Is there enough bread to share?
4. Why is "They smiled a lot of" incorrect?

## Summary
• Use a lot of before a noun.
• Use a lot when no noun follows.
• Write a lot as two words, and do not add an s to lot.

### Answers to practice
1. There is a lot of kindness here, and the children help a lot.
2. a lot of guests
3. Yes, there is enough bread to share. (or a true full-sentence no)
4. A lot of needs a noun. Say they smiled a lot, or they smiled a lot of smiles only if you really mean that noun.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Using both patterns in speech and writing
studyPages.body:
LESSON 3: USING BOTH PATTERNS IN SPEECH AND WRITING
===================================================

## What you will learn
• Combine both language patterns in a short piece of writing.
• Answer questions about the patterns in complete sentences.
• Choose these patterns on purpose when you speak.

Curriculum outcomes: b) respond to questions on the language patterns in written communication; c) adopt the use of language structures for effective communication

## Introduction
A pattern you only meet on a worksheet stays fragile. A pattern you use to thank a guest, or to describe your class, becomes part of your English. This lesson puts both patterns to work.

## Notes
### A short model
Read this paragraph aloud.

Our class has enough patience to listen when one person speaks. There are enough chairs to seat every learner. We use a lot of polite words, and those words help us a lot. I have enough courage to say sorry when I am wrong.

Patterns in the model:

- enough patience to listen
- enough chairs to seat
- a lot of polite words
- help us a lot
- enough courage to say

Nothing in the paragraph is there only as decoration. Each sentence could be said in a real classroom.

### Questions to answer in writing
Write the answer in a full sentence.

1. Do you have enough time to help a classmate today?
2. Are there enough pencils to share in your group?
3. Is there a lot of noise, or a lot of quiet, when everyone uses quiet voices?
4. Do polite words matter a lot? Why?

Sample answer for 4: Yes, polite words matter a lot because they show respect and keep the class peaceful.

Your answers should be true for your group. If there are not enough pencils, say so with the pattern: No, there are not enough pencils to share.

### Speak the patterns
With a partner, take turns.

- Ask: Do we have enough water to offer a visitor?
- Answer in the pattern.
- Ask: Do we say thank you a lot?
- Answer: Yes, we say thank you a lot. / We need to say thank you a lot more often.

Correct a slipped pattern kindly. If a partner says "enough of chairs to sit", you can reply, "Let us say enough chairs to seat our group."

### Make them a habit
Adopting a language structure means choosing it again tomorrow, not only in this exercise. When you write a story about a visitor, you might include one sentence with enough and one with a lot of. When you speak at home, "Is there enough food to share?" is both good English and good manners.

Correct sentences help people trust your meaning. A muddled pattern makes the listener rebuild your idea. Clear patterns are part of effective communication.

## Key words
• model — a correct piece of language you can follow
• adopt — to take up a habit and keep using it
• complete sentence — a sentence that gives a full answer, not a single word

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Join these ideas in one correct sentence: many polite words / they help the class greatly.

Working:
1. Many or much before a noun can be said with a lot of.
2. Greatly, at the end, can be said with a lot.

Answer: We use a lot of polite words, and they help the class a lot.

### Example 2
A learner writes "I have enough sorry to say." What should change?

Working:
1. Sorry is not the noun that fits this meaning.
2. The noun is words or courage. The infinitive is to say sorry.

Answer: I have enough words to say sorry. Or: I have enough courage to say sorry.

## Activity: Write and answer
You will need: Exercise book, The poem and the model paragraph
1. Copy the model paragraph in your best print.
2. Underline every example of enough + noun + to + verb, and of a lot or a lot of.
3. Answer the four questions in the notes in full sentences that are true for your group.
4. With a partner, ask and answer two spoken questions using the patterns. Help each other keep the word order.

## Practice
1. Rewrite correctly: We have enough of cups to serve a lots of guest.
2. Answer in a full sentence: Do polite words matter a lot?
3. Write one sentence that contains both enough + noun + to + verb and a lot of.
4. Why should you keep using these patterns after the lesson?

## Summary
• Enough + noun + to + verb shows that an amount is sufficient for a purpose.
• A lot of comes before a noun. A lot stands without one.
• Full-sentence answers keep the pattern visible and the meaning clear.

### Answers to practice
1. We have enough cups to serve a lot of guests.
2. Yes, polite words matter a lot because they show respect.
3. Any correct sentence, for example: We have enough time to welcome a lot of visitors.
4. So that your speech and writing stay clear, and so that the patterns become a habit.

questions.question: Which sentence follows enough + noun + to + verb?
options: We have enough water to offer a guest.
We have to enough water offer.
We enough have water a guest.
questions.explanation: Enough comes before the noun, and to comes before the verb.

questions.question: Which line from the poem uses the enough pattern?
options: We have enough bread to share at the meal.
A lot of polite words make visitors glad.
questions.explanation: Enough bread to share is enough + noun + infinitive.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: There are enough plate to serve.
There are enough plates to serve.
There is enough plates to serve.
There are a enough plates to serve.
questions.explanation: Plates is plural, so use are, and enough comes before plates.

questions.question: Which phrase is correct?
questions.explanation: A lot of is two words plus of, and lot has no s.

questions.question: The children help ____.
questions.explanation: No noun follows, so the phrase is a lot.

questions.question: There is ____ kindness in this home.
questions.explanation: Kindness is a noun, so use a lot of.

questions.question: Answer the question in a full sentence: Is there enough bread to share?
questions.answer: Yes, there is enough bread to share.
questions.explanation: A full answer repeats the pattern instead of stopping at yes.

questions.question: What is wrong with "I have enough sorry to say"?
questions.answer: Sorry should be part of the infinitive or the purpose, not the noun. Say: I have enough words to say sorry.
questions.explanation: The noun names what you have enough of. The infinitive names the purpose.

questions.question: Which sentence uses both patterns correctly?
options: We have enough time to welcome a lot of visitors.
We have a lot time to enough welcome.
Enough we have visitors a lot of to welcome.
We a lot of have enough.
questions.explanation: Enough time to welcome is the first pattern, and a lot of visitors is the second.

questions.question: Why do these patterns help communication?
questions.answer: They show amount and purpose clearly, so the listener does not have to rebuild your meaning.
questions.explanation: A correct pattern is easier to understand than a muddled one.
